titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Félez Muñoz sent along; Avengalvón learns of the plot and threatens the Infantes (tiradas 126–127, lines 2618–2680)
part: Tiradas 126–127 · Félez Muñoz sent along; Avengalvón learns of the plot and threatens the Infantes (lines 2618–2680)

sentences.t:
“¿O eres mio sobrino, tú, Félez Muñoz,
primo eres de mis fijas amas d’ alma e de coraçón!
sentences.l:
“Where are-you my nephew, you, Félez Muñoz,
cousin you-are of my daughters both from soul and from heart!
sentences.i: “Where are you, my nephew, Félez Muñoz? You are cousin to both my daughters, with all your soul and heart!
sentences.n: Tirada 126 (assonance ó) — the Çid sends Félez Muñoz with his daughters; the last farewell, and the Çid turns back to Valencia; the travellers reach Molina, and Avengalvón escorts them to Medinaceli; the Infantes plan to kill Avengalvón (Pidal: El Cid envía con sus hijas a Félez Muñoz. — Último adiós. El Cid torna a Valencia. — Los viajeros llegan a Molina. Abengalvón les acompaña a Medina. — Los infantes piensan matar a Abengalvón). The line-ends run Muñoz, coraçón, Carrión, son, Campeador …: stressed ó, now and then with an e after it (avorozes, v. 2649). The Çid speaks; the verse opens “¿O eres … with Pidal's ¿ and no closing ? anywhere: the question is the call itself, 'where are you?', O = ó, 'where' (Latin ubi), as in “¿O sodes, Raquel e Vidas …” (v. 102) and o dizen 'where they call' (v. 2657). eres, 'you are'; tú, the familiar singular, as befits a young kinsman. Félez Muñoz, the Çid's nephew (named among his knights at v. 741). primo eres de mis fijas, 'you are cousin to my daughters'; amas = ambas, 'both'. d' alma e de coraçón, 'from soul and from heart', wholeheartedly, a formula Félez himself takes up at v. 2623. The line closes with ! and no ¡, as printed.

sentences.i: I bid you go with them right into Carrión: you will see the lands that have been given to my daughters, and come back with the news to the Campeador.”
sentences.n: Mándot = mándote, te mando, 'I order you', the te cut to t. vayas, present subjunctive, 'that you go'. fata = hasta, 'as far as' (f- for modern h-); fata dentro en Carrión, 'right inside Carrión'. heredades, 'estates, inherited lands': the arras the Infantes settled on their brides (vv. 2564-5). dadas son, 'are given', the passive with ser. aquestas = estas. vernás, future of venir (= vendrás), 'you will come'. The Çid speaks of himself in the third person, al Campeador. The speech closes here.

sentences.t: Dixo Félez Muñoz: “plazme d’ alma e de coraçón.”
sentences.l: Said Félez Muñoz: “it-pleases-me from soul and from heart.”
sentences.i: Félez Muñoz said: “It pleases me with all my soul and heart.”
sentences.n: plazme = me plaze (me place), 'it pleases me', the pronoun after the verb at the head of the clause. d' alma e de coraçón, the Çid's own words of v. 2619 given back to him.

sentences.t:
Minaya Álbar Fáñez ante mio Çid se paró:
“Tornémosnos, Çid, a Valençia la mayor;
que si a Dios ploguiere e al Padre Criador,
ir las hemos ve[de]r a tierras de Carrión.”
sentences.i: Minaya Álvar Fáñez drew up before my Çid: “Let us turn back, Çid, to Valencia the great; for, if it please God and the Father Creator, we will go to see them in the lands of Carrión.”
sentences.n: Minaya Álbar Fáñez, 'Minaya Álvar Fáñez' in the English (house rendering). se paró, 'stopped, halted' (pararse), drawing rein before the Çid. Tornémosnos, 'let us turn back', the present subjunctive tornemos with nos, one s dropped (= tornémonos). Valençia la mayor, 'Valencia the great', the city's standing epithet. ploguiere, future subjunctive of plazer, 'if it should please'. Pidal's note to v. 2626: 'a Dios e al Padre, comp. v. 300' — the same pious doublet as Dios e … el Padre spirital there: God the Father, the Creator. ir las hemos ve[de]r, the split future: the infinitive ir, then the pronoun las, then hemos, 'we will go to see them' (= las iremos a ver), with ver as a bare infinitive after a verb of motion. ve[de]r = veder, the old full form of ver: the d is clearly Pidal's italic, the e very probably so too, and the exact extent of the italic is not certain.

sentences.t:
—“A Dios vos acomendamos, don Elvira e doña Sol
atales cosas fed que en plazer caya a nos.”
sentences.l:
—“To God you we-commend, don Elvira and doña Sol
such things do that in pleasure may-fall to us.”
sentences.i: —“We commend you to God, Doña Elvira and Doña Sol; act in such a way that it brings us joy.”
sentences.n: Pidal opens the line with a dash and a quotation mark (—“), a new speaker; the plural acomendamos, 'we commend', speaks for the Çid and those with him, and who exactly says it is not stated (most likely the Çid). acomendamos = encomendamos (cf. acomiendo, v. 371). don Elvira, so printed, with don before a woman's name; 'Doña Elvira' in the English, as elsewhere. v. 2628 ends without punctuation, as printed. atales = tales, 'such', printed as one word. fed, imperative plural of fer (fazer), 'do' (= haced). caya = caiga, present subjunctive of caer, 'fall'. Pidal's note to v. 2629: 'haced tales cosas que nos sea motivo de placer' — 'do such things as may be a cause of pleasure to us'. The farewell asks them to bring honour on the house.

sentences.t: Respondien los yernos: “assí lo mande Dios!”
sentences.l: Were-answering the sons-in-law: “so it may-command God!”
sentences.i: The sons-in-law answered: “May God so ordain it!”
sentences.n: Respondien = respondían, 'were answering', imperfect for a single act, the epic mixing of tenses. yernos, 'sons-in-law', the Infantes. assí lo mande Dios, present subjunctive, 'so may God ordain it': a pious answer from men who mean the opposite. The line closes with ! and no ¡, as printed.

sentences.t:
Grandes fueron los duelos a la departiçión.
El padre con las fijas lloran de coraçón,
assí fazían los cavalleros del Campeador.
sentences.l:
Great were the griefs at the parting.
The father with the daughters weep from heart,
so were-doing the knights of-the Campeador.
sentences.i: Great was the grief at the parting. Father and daughters weep from the heart, and so did the Campeador's knights.
sentences.n: duelos, 'griefs, laments' (duelo). departiçión, 'parting, separation'. El padre con las fijas lloran, 'the father with the daughters weep': the verb plural, agreeing with the sense (father and daughters together). de coraçón, 'from the heart'. Pidal's note to v. 2633: 'assí fazían, "lo mismo hacían"' — 'they did the same'. fazían = hacían, f- for modern h-.

sentences.t:
“Oyas, sobrino, tú, Félez Muñoz!
por Molina iredes, i yazredes una noch;
sentences.l:
“Hear, nephew, you, Félez Muñoz!
by Molina you-will-go, there you-will-lie one night;
sentences.i: “Listen, nephew, Félez Muñoz! You will go by way of Molina and rest there for a night;
sentences.n: The Çid speaks again to his nephew. Oyas, present subjunctive of oír, used as a command, 'hear, listen'. The line closes with ! and no ¡, as printed. iredes = iréis, 'you will go', the old -edes ending of the second person plural (here addressed to the whole party). i = allí, 'there'. yazredes, future of yazer (yacer), 'you will lie', i.e. 'lodge, rest' (= yaceréis). Pidal's note to v. 2635: 'allí descansaréis una noche' — 'there you will rest one night'. noch = noche. Molina, Molina de Aragón, the town held by the Çid's Moorish friend Avengalvón (vv. 1462–4).

sentences.t:
saludad a mio amigo el moro Avengalvón:
reciba a mios yernos commo ell[e] pudier mejor;
sentences.l:
greet for-me my friend the Moor Avengalvón:
let-him-receive my sons-in-law as he could best;
sentences.i: greet my friend the Moor Avengalvón for me: let him receive my sons-in-law as best he can;
sentences.n: saludad, imperative plural, 'greet'. Avengalvón, the Moorish lord of Molina, the Çid's friend 'in peace' (v. 1464), who escorted Ximena and the daughters to Valencia (tiradas 83–86); spelled Avengalvón here, Ave[n]galvón (the n Pidal's) earlier. reciba, present subjunctive, 'let him receive'. ell[e] = él, 'he', with an added -e, the e Pidal's. pudier = pudiere, future subjunctive of poder, 'as best he may be able'.

sentences.t:
dil que enbío mis fijas a tierras de Carrión,
de lo que ovieren huebos sírvalas a so sabor,
desí escúrralas fasta Medina por la mi amor.
sentences.l:
tell-him that I-send my daughters to lands of Carrión,
of what they-may-have need let-him-serve-them at their pleasure,
then let-him-escort-them as-far-as Medina for the my love.
sentences.i: tell him that I am sending my daughters to the lands of Carrión; whatever they need, let him serve them as they please, and then escort them as far as Medinaceli, for love of me.
sentences.n: dil = dile, imperative of dezir + le, 'tell him'. enbío = envío, 'I send'. de lo que ovieren huebos, 'of what they may have need': aver huebos (Latin opus), 'to need'; ovieren, future subjunctive of aver. Pidal's note to v. 2639: 'Véase 1878, "deles lo que necesiten"' — 'give them what they need'. sírvalas, present subjunctive + las, 'let him serve them'; a so sabor, 'to their liking', so = su. desí, 'then, after that'. escúrralas, present subjunctive of escurrir + las: Pidal's note to v. 2640: 'después acompáñelas (v. 1067) hasta Medinaceli' — 'then let him accompany them as far as Medinaceli'. escurrir here is 'escort' in the English too, not a farewell 'see off': the escort goes with them for a day's ride. Medina is Medinaceli, the farthest limit of Alfonso's realm. por la mi amor, 'for my love', 'for love of me': amor feminine, as often in Old Spanish, with article + possessive.

sentences.t: De quanto él fiziere yol dar[é] por ello buen galardón.”
sentences.l: Of all-that he may-do I-to-him will-give for it good reward.”
sentences.i: For all he does I will give him a good reward.”
sentences.n: De quanto él fiziere, 'of all that he may do', fiziere future subjunctive of fazer. yol = yo le, 'I … to him'. dar[é], future of dar, the é Pidal's. galardón, 'reward'. The Çid's speech closes here; Pidal's repeated line-initial quote on this line is dropped, as throughout.

sentences.t:
Quomo la uña de la carne ellos partidos son.
Yas tornó pora Valençia el que en buen ora nasçió.
sentences.l:
As the nail from the flesh they parted are.
Now-himself turned for Valençia he who in good hour was-born.
sentences.i: As the nail is torn from the flesh, so they parted. And now he who was born in a good hour turned back to Valencia.
sentences.n: Quomo = commo, como, 'as', in a rare spelling. la uña de la carne, 'the nail from the flesh', the proverbial image of a parting that tears (cf. v. 375, when the Çid left Ximena at San Pedro de Cardeña). partidos son, 'they are parted', the perfect of a verb of motion with ser. Yas = ya + se, 'now … himself': tornarse, 'to turn back'. pora = para. el que en buen ora nasçió, the en buen ora formula, 'he who was born in a good hour' (house rendering): the Çid.

sentences.i: The Infantes of Carrión set out on their way; at Santa María de Albarracín they made their halt for the night; the Infantes of Carrión spur on as hard as they can; and there they are in Molina with the Moor Avengalvón.
sentences.n: Piénssanse de ir, 'they set about going', penssar(se) de + infinitive, 'to set about, make ready to'. ifantes de Carrión, without the article, as often. Pidal's note to v. 2645: 'Para Alvarrazín véase 1462': there he explains Santa María as today's Albarracín (province of Teruel), named for the Muslim family of the Aben Razín who held it. la posada [fecho fo], 'the lodging was made', the night's halt: fecho fo (hecho fue) is wholly Pidal's restoration, in italics; the masculine fecho with feminine posada is as printed. aguijan, 'they spur on' (aguijar, to goad). félos = he + los, 'behold them, there they are' (cf. felos en Medina, v. 1452). Epic tense-mixing: preterite fo, present aguijan.

sentences.i: The Moor, when he learned of it, was glad with all his heart; he came out to receive them with great rejoicing. God, how well he served them, entirely to their liking!
sentences.n: sopo, preterite of saber, 'learned, came to know'. plógol = le plogo (le plugo), preterite of plazer + le, 'it pleased him'. saliólos recebir = salió a recibirlos, 'went out to receive them', the bare infinitive after a verb of motion, the pronoun drawn onto salió. Pidal's note to v. 2649: 'avorozes, "alborozos, regocijos"' — 'rejoicings'; avorozes ends in ó-e, a licit variant of the ó assonance. Dios, que bien = ¡Dios, qué bien!, 'God, how well', the minstrel's exclamation; the line closes with ! and no ¡, as printed. a todo so sabor, 'wholly to their liking'.

sentences.t:
Otro día mañana con ellos cavalgó,
con dozientos cavalleros escurrir los mandó;
sentences.l:
Next day morning with them he-rode,
with two-hundred knights to-escort them he-ordered;
sentences.i: Next morning he rode with them, and had two hundred knights escort them on their way;
sentences.n: Otro día mañana, 'the next day, in the morning'. cavalgó, 'rode'. escurrir los mandó, 'he ordered (them) to escort them', the bare infinitive after mandar, the pronoun los (the travellers) set between: he gave them an escort of two hundred knights, as the Çid had asked (v. 2640, Pidal 'acompáñelas'). Pidal has no note here; escurrir is 'escort' in the English as well, for this is the escort on the road, not the leave-taking. He rides with them himself (v. 2672).

sentences.t:
ivan troçir los montes, los que dizen de Luzón,
troçieron Arbuxuelo e llegaron a Salón,
o dizen el Anssarera ellos posados son.
sentences.l:
they-were-going to-cross the mountains, those that they-call of Luzón,
they-crossed Arbuxuelo and arrived at Salón,
where they-call the Anssarera they lodged are.
sentences.i: They went on to cross the mountains they call the Luzón hills; they passed through the Arbujuelo valley and came to the Jalón, and they took their lodging at the place called the Ansarera.
sentences.n: Order: Pidal prints vv. 2656–2657 before vv. 2654–2655, keeping all four numbers; his print order and numbers are followed here. Pidal's note to v. 2653: 'iban a atravesar los montes; son las montañas fieras e grandes del v. 1491' — 'they went on to cross the mountains; they are the "wild and high mountains" of v. 1491'. ivan troçir, 'were going to cross', ir + bare infinitive; troçir, 'to pass, cross'. los que dizen de Luzón, 'those they call (the mountains) of Luzón'; Pidal says no more of Luzón. Pidal's note to v. 2656: 'pasaron el valle de Arbujuelo; v. 1493'. Arbuxuelo, 'Arbujuelo' in the English, as earlier; Salón is the river Jalón, which runs below Medinaceli. o = donde, 'where' (as in v. 2618). Pidal's note to v. 2657: 'el Ansarera es lugar hoy desconocido, que tenía que estar situado entre Medinaceli y el río Jalón' — 'el Ansarera is a place unknown today, which must have lain between Medinaceli and the river Jalón'. posados son, 'they are lodged'.

sentences.i: To the Çid's daughters the Moor gave his gifts, and a good horse apiece to the Infantes of Carrión; all this the Moor did for them out of love for the Çid Campeador.
sentences.n: These two lines (2654–2655) stand after v. 2657 in Pidal's print (see the previous note). donas, 'gifts' (Latin dona). dió, accented as printed. Pidal's note to v. 2655: 'sendos caballos buenos' — 'a good horse each': seños = sendos, 'one each'. tod esto = todo esto, 'all this'. por el amor del Çid, 'out of love for the Çid', amor masculine here (cf. la mi amor, v. 2640). Campead[or], the o and r Pidal's.

sentences.t:
Ellos ve[d]ien la riqueza que el moro sacó,
entramos hermanos conssejaron traçión:
sentences.l:
They were-seeing the wealth that the Moor brought-out,
both brothers plotted treason:
sentences.i: They saw the riches the Moor brought out, and the two brothers plotted treachery:
sentences.n: ve[d]ien = veían, imperfect of veer (ver), 'were seeing', the d Pidal's. sacó, 'brought out', displayed in giving his gifts. Pidal's note to v. 2660: 'ambos hermanos maquinaron traición' — 'both brothers plotted treachery'. entramos = entrambos, 'both'. conssejaron, 'took counsel on, plotted' (conssejar). traçión = traición.

sentences.t:
“Ya pues que a dexar avemos fijas del Campeador,
si pudiéssemos matar el moro Avengalvón,
quanta riquiza tiene aver la yemos nos.
sentences.i: “Now, since we are to abandon the Campeador's daughters, if we could kill the Moor Avengalvón, we would have all the wealth he owns.
sentences.n: Ya pues que, 'now, since'. a dexar avemos, aver a + infinitive, 'we have to abandon', 'we are to leave': the plan of tirada 124 named outright. fijas del Campeador, without the article. matar el moro, the object without the personal a. riquiza, 'wealth', so printed (riqueza at v. 2659). aver la yemos, the split conditional: the infinitive aver, then the pronoun la (the riquiza), then yemos (= íamos), 'we would have it' (= la habríamos); nos, 'we', set at the end for stress.

sentences.t:
Tan en salvo lo abremos commo lo de Carrión;
nunqua avrié derecho de nos el Çid Campeador.”
sentences.l:
As in safety it we-will-have as that of Carrión;
never would-have redress from us the Çid Campeador.”
sentences.i: We shall hold it as safely as our own lands of Carrión, and the Çid Campeador would never have redress from us.”
sentences.n: Tan en salvo … commo, 'as safe … as'; abremos = avremos, 'we will have, hold'; lo de Carrión, 'what is in Carrión', their own lands. avrié, conditional of aver, 'would have'. Pidal's note to v. 2665: 'nunca lograría reparación de nuestra parte, es decir, quedaríamos impunes' — 'he would never obtain reparation from us, that is to say, we should go unpunished'. derecho, 'right, justice, redress'. The speech closes here.

sentences.i: While the men of Carrión were speaking this treachery, a Moor who knew the Christians' tongue understood it all; he did not keep the secret, but told it to Avengalvón:
sentences.n: falssedad, 'falsehood, treachery'. dizien = dezían, 'were saying'. los de Carrión, 'those of Carrión', the Infantes. Pidal's note to v. 2667: 'latinado, "ladino, que sabe la lengua romance"' — 'ladino, who knows the Romance tongue': latín here is the Romance spoken by the Christians, which the Infantes assumed no Moor would follow. gelo = ge lo (se lo), 'it … (to) him', the plotters' words; bien … entendió, 'understood well'. non tiene poridad, 'he keeps no secret', poridad 'secret, privacy'. díxolo = lo dixo, 'told it'; Avengalvón, the person told, without the a.

sentences.t:
“Acáyaz, cúriate destos, ca eres mio señor:
tu muert o[d]i co[n]ssejar a ifantes de Carrión.”
sentences.l:
“Governor, guard-yourself from-these, for you-are my lord:
your death I-heard plot to Infantes of Carrión.”
sentences.i: “Governor, be on your guard against these men, for you are my lord: I heard the Infantes of Carrión plotting your death.”
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 2669: 'Acáyaz, "alcaide", lo mismo que alcayaz, 1502' — 'commander of a fortress', the same as alcáyaz at v. 1502, where Avengalvón was called by this title: 'governor' in the English, as there. cúriate, imperative of curiar + te, 'guard yourself' (cf. curiar, v. 2569). destos = de estos, 'from these'. ca, 'for'. o[d]i = oí, 'I heard' (from odir, the d restored): the d is Pidal's italic and the o looks roman, though the exact extent is not certain. co[n]ssejar, 'plot, counsel', the n Pidal's; the bare infinitive after a verb of perceiving, with a ifantes de Carrión its subject, 'I heard the Infantes plotting'. The speech closes here, and with it the tirada.

sentences.t:
El moro Avengalvón, mucho era buen barragán,
co[n] dozientos que tiene iva cavalgar;
sentences.l:
The Moor Avengalvón, very he-was good stout-fellow,
with two-hundred that he-has went to-ride;
sentences.i: The Moor Avengalvón was a right valiant man: with the two hundred men he had, he rode up;
sentences.n: Tirada 127 (assonance á / á-e) — Avengalvón takes his leave, threatening the Infantes (Pidal: Abengalbón se despide amenazando a los infantes). The line-ends run barragán, cavalgar, ifantes, plaze, Bivar, sonás, leal, jamás: stressed á, sometimes with an e after it. Pidal's note to v. 2671: 'buen barragán, "buen mozo", "esforzado"; compárese 3327' — 'a fine young fellow', 'valiant'. mucho era buen barragán, 'he was a very good, a right valiant man'. co[n], the n Pidal's. con dozientos que tiene, 'with the two hundred (knights) he has' (v. 2652). iva cavalgar, ir + bare infinitive, 'went riding, rode on'.

sentences.t:
armas iva teniendo, parós ante los ifantes;
de lo que el moro dixo a los ifantes non plaze:
sentences.l:
arms he-went holding, stopped-himself before the Infantes;
of what the Moor said to the Infantes not it-pleases:
sentences.i: he came playing at arms and drew up before the Infantes; what the Moor said to the Infantes was not to their liking:
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 2673: 'iba jugando las armas, v. 1577' — 'he went playing at arms': armas iva teniendo, the display of horsemanship and mock combat (cf. teniendo … armas, v. 2613), here with an edge of menace. parós = se paró, 'halted, stood'. de lo que … non plaze, 'of what the Moor said, (it) does not please the Infantes': present plaze among the preterites. Pidal's numbering jumps here: vv. 2675–2676 are printed by him at the head of tirada 128, where the same speech goes on, and they belong to the next part.

sentences.t:
“Si no lo dexás por mio Çid el de Bivar,
tal cosa vos faría que por el mundo sonás,
sentences.l:
“If not it I-left for my Çid the one of Bivar,
such thing to-you I-would-do that through the world it-might-resound,
sentences.i: “If I did not hold back for the sake of my Çid of Vivar, I would do you such a thing that it would ring through all the world;
sentences.n: dexás and sonás, at the line-ends, are read as imperfect subjunctives with their final e dropped (dexás[e], sonás[e]): 'if I did not leave it (alone)', 'that it should resound'; Pidal gives no note, and the reading is not certain. no, so printed, not non. por mio Çid el de Bivar, 'for my Çid's sake, the one of Vivar'. faría, conditional of fer (fazer), 'I would do'. por el mundo, 'through the world'.

sentences.t:
e luego levaría sus fijas al Campeador leal;
vos nu[n]qua en Carrión entrariedes jamás.
sentences.l:
and at-once I-would-take his daughters to-the Campeador loyal;
you never in Carrión would-enter ever.
sentences.i: and I would take his daughters straight back to the loyal Campeador; and you would never set foot in Carrión again.
sentences.n: luego, 'at once'. levaría = llevaría, 'I would take', conditional. al Campeador leal, 'to the loyal Campeador', back to their father. nu[n]qua … jamás, 'never … ever', the double negative of emphasis; the second n of nunqua is Pidal's. entrariedes = entraríais, conditional, 'you would enter'. The speech has no closing quotation mark: it runs on into tirada 128, which Pidal opens with vv. 2675–2676 (“¿Dezidme, qué vos fiz …”) and which belongs to the next part.
